newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila to take office on Thursday, showdown looms.
newsitem.headline: Kabila to take office on Thursday, showdown looms.

text.p: Self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila will formally take office on Thursday as head of state of the Democratic Republic of Congo -- one day after a looming showdown with Kinshasa's political opposition.

State radio and television said that Kabila, whose forces marched into the capital on May 17, would take office in a ceremony at the People's Palace parliament building and that the inauguration would be his "first official outing".

Earlier, opposition militants defied a ban on political activity to announce at a news conference that they would take to the streets on Wednesday to demand greater political dialogue and the withdrawal of foreign forces.

In South Africa, President Nelson Mandela accused Western governments of demonising Kabila and said that his ban on political activity, announced on state television on Monday, was understandable in the circumstances.
"You must judge what president Kabila is doing against the specific conditions existing in that country," Mandela said during a visit by Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni.

"There is a great deal of disorganisation in that country. It would be suicidal for him to allow the operation of parties before he has a firm grip on the government of the country," he told reporters.
"It does appear to me that he has been so demonised by Western governments that even his achievements have not been noticed," he said.
Aides said Kabila would join other African presidents at the Organisation of African Unity annual summit in Zimbabwe at the start of June.
There was little immediate response in Kinshasa on Tuesday to the ban on politics and demonstrations. Shops, offices and markets opened. Traffic circulated normally.
Opposition activists promised protests this week and next.

"Despite the ban, there will be a democratic march tomorrow," Jean-Marie Vianney Kabukanye, national secretary of the youth wing of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi said.

"We have not changed Mobutu to replace him with another Mobutu. The man has changed but not the policies," he told Reuters in the opposition stronghold of Limete. Kabila's forces did not try to prevent him giving a news conference.
The statement announcing the ban said anyone infringing it would be considered an "enemy of the liberation of the people". It said that the ban would apply until further notice.

"We haven't banned the parties, they exist but they cannot carry out any activities," information ministry spokesman Leyka Moussa Nyembo told Reuters. "The parties stop being active until we have restored a bit of order," he said.
He said the ban was effectively nationwide as it was already in force in the rest of Africa's third largest nation.
Opposition activists marched in Kinshasa on Friday and Saturday. Kabila forces fired in the air and took away some protesters. Government officials said they were later released.
Tshisekedi, citing a 1992 vote in a sovereign national conference in what was then Zaire, has doggedly insisted over the years that constitutionally he is prime minister.
Kabila's ministers accuse Tshisekedi of deluding the people to feed his own ambition.
Tshisekedi aides say Kabila has flooded the capital with troops from Rwanda and other neighbours and accuse him of seeking to return to a one-party state.
"Foreign troops must leave as soon as possible or risk appearing like occupation troops," Vianney said.
Kabila aides say he plans to increase the number of cabinet ministers to 20 from 13 but without appointing a prime minister.
